itens.resumo: Spanish Jesuit, companion of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, known as the "Apostle of the Orient" for his evangelizing mission in India, Southeast Asia and Japan; universal patron of the missions.
itens.corpo:
Francis de Jasso y Azpilicueta was born on April 7, 1506, in the castle of Xavier, in the then independent Kingdom of Navarre, the son of a noble family: his father, Juan de Jasso, was a doctor of law from the University of Bologna, president of the Royal Council of Navarre and counselor to King John III. Shortly after the birth of his son, the Castilian war of annexation ruined and partially dismantled the family's castle and lands. While still young, he left to study at the University of Paris, where he earned a master of arts at the Collège de Sainte-Barbe and shared a room with an older Basque soldier, Ignatius of Loyola, who only after months of insistence — and of the question that would become famous, about what it profits a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul — managed to win him over to the plan of life that was maturing.

On August 15, 1534, Francis Xavier was one of the first seven companions who, in the crypt of the chapel of Saint-Denis, in Montmartre, took vows of poverty, chastity and of making a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, placing themselves at the disposal of the pope to be sent wherever the need was greatest — the founding nucleus of what would become, in 1540, the Society of Jesus, of which Xavier was a co-founder. Ordained a priest in Venice in 1537, he remained in Rome as one of Ignatius's closest collaborators until, in 1540, King John III of Portugal asked the pope for Jesuit missionaries for the East; chosen at the last minute to replace a companion who had fallen ill, he sailed from Lisbon on April 7, 1541, the day he turned 35, as apostolic nuncio for the Indies.

He arrived in Goa in May 1542 and began, in the following months, his work among the Paravas, pearl fishers of the Fishery Coast in southern India, who converted en masse to Christianity; without mastering their languages, Xavier went through the villages ringing a bell, gathering children and catechizing by means of rudimentary translations of the catechism, the Our Father and the Creed. This method of numerous and rapid baptisms, however, would later be the object of criticism regarding the solidity of the religious instruction of the converts — a question common to the history of the missions of the period. In the following years he extended his work to Cochin, Travancore, Malacca and the Moluccas — reaching Ambon, Ternate and Morotai —, always in precarious conditions, often alone. In Goa he directed the College of Saint Paul, which trained Asian catechists and clergy and promoted the translation of religious books into the local languages. His correspondence, written over eleven years in the East, became a fundamental source for the history of Jesuit missionary expansion and achieved enormous diffusion in Europe during his lifetime.

It was in Malacca, in 1547, that Xavier met Anjirō (Yajirō), a Japanese samurai fugitive who sought to purify himself of a homicide and who awakened in him the desire to evangelize Japan, then practically unknown to Europeans. He took Anjirō to Goa, where he baptized him and prepared him as an interpreter, and set out with him, with Father Cosme de Torres and Brother Juan Fernández for the archipelago. Aboard the junk of the Chinese pirate Awan, the three Jesuits landed at Kagoshima on August 15, 1549, the feast of the Assumption. In Japan, Xavier quickly realized that the success of the mission depended on adapting to local customs: he began to dress in dignified clothing, to carry gifts and to seek audience with the feudal lords (daimyos) before preaching to the people, a method that gained him access to the court of Ōuchi Yoshitaka in Yamaguchi and to nascent Christian communities in Hirado, Yamaguchi and Bungo (present-day Funai). A letter written in Kagoshima in November 1549, with his first impressions of the archipelago, was published in Coimbra in 1551 and in Rome and Venice the following year; in it Xavier called the Japanese "the best people yet discovered." Still in Japan, the initial translation of the term "God" as Dainichi — a word linked to Buddhism — caused confusion among the local monks, forcing the missionary to revise his terminology.

After about two years and three months in Japan, Xavier left the young mission in the care of Torres and Fernández and returned to Goa in early 1552, already planning a new challenge: to enter China, then closed to foreigners, to evangelize the empire whose cultural superiority the Japanese themselves acknowledged. He traveled to the island of Sancian (Shangchuan), near the coast of Canton, hoping to obtain clandestine passage to the mainland, but fell ill with fevers and died there, practically alone, on December 3, 1552, without ever having set foot on Chinese soil.

His body was initially buried on the island and exhumed in February 1553; taken first to the Church of Saint Paul in Malacca, it was transferred to Goa, where it arrived in early 1554 and was exposed to public veneration from March 16 to 18 of that year. Found in a state that accounts of the time described as incorrupt, it remains venerated to this day in the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Old Goa, on public exposition every ten years; in 1614 his right forearm — used, according to tradition, to baptize and bless tens of thousands of people in Asia — was separated as a relic and sent to Rome, where it is found in the Church of the Gesù. Beatified on October 25, 1619, by Pope Paul V, he was canonized on March 12, 1622, by Pope Gregory XV, in the same ceremony that raised Ignatius of Loyola, Teresa of Ávila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer to the altars. On December 14, 1927, Pope Pius XI declared him universal patron of the Catholic missions, together with Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus; his feast is celebrated on December 3.

itens.resumo: Italian Jesuit missionary who introduced Christianity to imperial China through the method of inculturation, adopting the Chinese language and customs.
itens.corpo:
Matteo Ricci was born in Macerata, in the Papal States, on October 6, 1552, and entered the Jesuit novitiate in Rome in 1571, at the age of nineteen. Between 1571 and 1577 he studied at the Roman College under the guidance of the mathematician and astronomer Christopher Clavius, receiving training not only in theology and philosophy, but also in mathematics, astronomy, cosmology, and cartography — a body of technical knowledge that, though he could not then foresee it, would become decisive for his future mission. Sent to the Far East, he arrived in Goa in 1578 and then in Macau in 1582, the Portuguese base from which the Jesuits had been trying, for years and without lasting success, to penetrate Chinese territory.

Already in Macau, Ricci and his superior Alessandro Valignano realized that the method then used in the Indies and in Japan — direct preaching and Western religious garb — would not work in a civilization that saw itself as the center of the civilized world and treated every foreigner as a barbarian. Ricci then devoted himself, with unusual discipline, to the study of classical Mandarin, the Confucian classics, and Chinese scholarly etiquette, eventually mastering writing to the point of composing texts and catechisms directly in Chinese; he initially adopted the robes of a Buddhist monk and, upon realizing that Confucian scholars enjoyed greater social prestige, began to dress like one of them, in a silk robe and with a long beard, a habit he would keep for the rest of his life.

This method, called "accommodation" or inculturation decades later, did not involve imposing Latin vocabulary and liturgy, but rather seeking bridges between Christian doctrine and Confucian ethics — a famous example is the very Chinese term Ricci chose for God, "Tianzhu" (Lord of Heaven), and his work The True Meaning of the Lord of Heaven (Tianzhu Shiyi), of 1603, which discusses philosophy and religion in the form of a dialogue with a fictional Chinese scholar. Ricci also used his scientific training as a point of entry: he presented mechanical clocks, prisms, astronomical instruments and, above all, in 1602, produced the Kunyu Wanguo Quantu ("Complete Map of the Myriad Countries of the World"), the first European-style world map printed in Chinese and the first cartographic representation to introduce the Americas to the Chinese public — an object of fascination at court that opened doors that preaching alone would never have opened.

After years of attempts and setbacks, traveling between Zhaoqing, Nanchang, and Nanjing, Ricci obtained authorization in January 1601 to enter the Forbidden City of Beijing and present himself at the court of the Wanli Emperor of the Ming dynasty, who was fascinated above all by the Western mechanical clocks the Jesuits brought as gifts. Although he was never received in person by the emperor, Ricci obtained permission to reside in the capital with an imperial stipend, becoming the first European to live in a stable and recognized manner within the inner circle of Chinese power; there he converted influential figures of the mandarin bureaucracy, among them the mathematician and high official Xu Guangqi, baptized Paul, with whom he translated into Chinese the first six books of Euclid's Elements.

Xu Guangqi, the official and cartographer Li Zhizao (baptized Leo), and the magistrate Yang Tingyun (baptized Michael) became known in the Chinese Catholic tradition as the "Three Pillars" of Catholicism in the country, each using his position in the scholarly elite to protect and spread the new faith and the scientific works the Jesuits brought with them; it was, moreover, with the technical collaboration of Li Zhizao that Ricci prepared the third and fourth expanded editions of his world map in 1603 and 1604.

Ricci died in Beijing on May 11, 1610, at the age of 57, and the emperor granted him an honor hitherto unprecedented for a foreigner: a burial plot on Chinese soil, today preserved within the campus of the Communist Party School in Beijing. He is considered the founder of the modern Catholic missions in China, and the method of inculturation he developed became, decades later, the center of the famous "Chinese Rites Controversy," when other orders questioned in Rome whether Ricci's ritual and terminological adaptations — such as allowing the veneration of ancestors and of Confucius — compromised Catholic doctrine; the dispute, which extended throughout the eighteenth century, ended with Rome's prohibition of the practices in 1704 and 1742, a blow that deeply weakened the Catholic presence in China for generations. His cause for canonization advanced slowly: in 2022 Pope Francis recognized his heroic virtues, declaring him Venerable.

itens.resumo: Spanish Jesuit known as the "Apostle of Brazil," catechist of the indigenous peoples and co-founder of the city of São Paulo.
itens.corpo:
José de Anchieta was born on March 19, 1534, in San Cristóbal de La Laguna, on Tenerife, in the Canary Islands, the son of a Basque nobleman exiled for taking part in a revolt against Charles V. He studied letters and philosophy at the College of Coimbra, in Portugal, where he entered the Society of Jesus in 1551, still an adolescent; a physical problem with his spine, which would stay with him all his life and leave him with a stooped posture, did not stop him from sailing two years later, in 1553, still a novice, for the Portuguese colony in America, as part of the expedition of Governor-General Duarte da Costa together with Father Manuel da Nóbrega, superior of the Jesuit mission in Brazil.

Having landed in Bahia, Anchieta was sent to the region of São Vicente and the plateau of Piratininga, where he revealed an uncommon talent for languages: he learned Tupi so thoroughly that, while still young, he began writing grammatical notes that would result, decades later, in the Arte de Gramática da Língua Mais Usada na Costa do Brasil (Art of Grammar of the Most Widely Used Language on the Coast of Brazil, 1595), the first systematic grammar of a Brazilian indigenous language and a fundamental tool for the catechesis carried out by the Jesuits who came after him. Besides the grammar, Anchieta produced an extensive multilingual body of work, in Portuguese, Castilian, Latin and Tupi, in prose and verse, including catechetical theatrical plays such as the Auto de São Lourenço and the prose chronicle De Gestis Mendi de Saa ("The Deeds of Mem de Sá"), using theater, music and poetry as deliberate strategies of evangelization adapted to the local culture, in a method that anticipates by decades later discussions on missionary inculturation. Anchieta was also the main author of, or a direct collaborator in, a set of catechetical texts in Tupi later gathered under the title Doutrina Cristã (Christian Doctrine), among them the Catecismo Brasílico (Brazilian Catechism) and the Diálogo da Fé (Dialogue of Faith), which reproduced in question-and-answer form the foundations of Christian doctrine and prayers such as the Our Father and the Hail Mary. Because the indigenous language had no exact equivalents for many Christian concepts, these works obliged him to create neologisms or import Portuguese terms adapted to Tupi phonetics.

On January 25, 1554, Anchieta was part of the group of twelve Jesuit priests and brothers, led by Nóbrega, who founded the Colégio de São Paulo de Piratininga (College of São Paulo de Piratininga) on top of a hill between the Anhangabaú and Tamanduateí rivers. It was a college-mission that would become the founding nucleus of the present-day city of São Paulo, which is why Anchieta is remembered to this day as one of the "founders" of the capital of São Paulo. In the following years he worked intensely in the catechesis of the Tupi-Guarani peoples, in the founding of other settlements, and in mediating between Portuguese colonists and indigenous populations, often dealing with situations of war and enslavement that marked the coast and the plateau in the second half of the sixteenth century.

One of the most remembered episodes of his life took place in 1563, during the Tamoio Confederation, an indigenous alliance that resisted Portuguese occupation: Anchieta and Nóbrega offered themselves as hostages in the village of Iperoig (present-day Ubatuba) to negotiate peace between the Tamoios and the colonizers, remaining for months at real risk of death. It was during this period of captivity, according to tradition, that Anchieta composed from memory, writing with a stick in the sand of the beach for lack of paper, his lengthy Poem to the Virgin Mary, in Latin, with nearly six thousand verses, which would only be transcribed onto paper months later, already in São Vicente; the negotiations at Iperoig resulted in a peace agreement that eased, although only temporarily, the conflict in the region.

Besides being a catechist and writer, Anchieta held a position of institutional leadership in the Society of Jesus in Brazil: he was superior of the Jesuit mission in the province and later Provincial of Brazil between 1577 and 1587, a period in which he oversaw the expansion of Jesuit colleges and residences along the coast. He spent the last years of his life in the village of Reritiba, in present-day Espírito Santo, where he died on June 9, 1597; in his honor, the locality was later renamed Anchieta. Beatified by Pope John Paul II on June 22, 1980, his sanctity was proclaimed by Pope Francis on April 3, 2014, through equipollent canonization, a process that dispenses with the usual confirmatory miracle when there is already an uninterrupted popular veneration consolidated over the centuries, and he is today venerated as the "Apostle of Brazil."

itens.resumo: A former French soldier and explorer who became a missionary hermit among the Tuareg of the Sahara Desert, proposing a mission of silent presence and universal fraternity.
itens.corpo:
Charles Eugène de Foucauld was born on September 15, 1858, in Strasbourg, into a noble family with a military tradition; orphaned of both father and mother at the age of six, he was raised by a grandfather and had a youth marked by excesses, spending, and a faith that he himself would later describe as completely lost. He graduated in 1876 from the Saint-Cyr military academy—where he earned the ironic nickname "Piggy" for the luxury with which he surrounded himself—, went on to the cavalry school at Saumur, and served as a cavalry officer in Algeria, from which he was dismissed for indiscipline, but to which he returned on his own initiative when his regiment was called up during a revolt, distinguishing himself then by his courage in combat.

It was in Algeria that his fascination with the Muslim world and the desert was born: between 1883 and 1884, disguised as a Jewish rabbi to avoid suspicion in a territory closed to Europeans, he carried out a dangerous geographical reconnaissance expedition through Morocco, then practically unexplored by Westerners, recorded in the book Reconnaissance au Maroc (1888), a work that earned him the gold medal of the Geographical Society of Paris. It was this journey, and his admiring contact with the deep faith and daily religious practice of the Muslims he met, that rekindled in him the religious question; back in Paris, in October 1886, under the guidance of Father Henri Huvelin—whom he sought out at the church of Saint-Augustin—he experienced a conversion that he described as instantaneous, upon going to confession and receiving Communion after years of estrangement: "As soon as I believed there was a God, I understood that I could do nothing else but live for Him," he would write later. In 1888-1889 he made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land.

Seeking a life of radicalism and self-effacement, in 1890 he entered the Trappists (Order of Cistercians of the Strict Observance) at the monastery of Notre-Dame des Neiges, then moved on to Akbès, in Syria, but felt that he was still seeking something poorer and closer to the Jesus of Nazareth who spent thirty years in obscurity before his public life. He left the Trappists in 1897 and lived as a handyman and then as a hermit next to a convent of Poor Clares in Nazareth, trying to reproduce in extreme poverty the "hidden life" of Jesus the craftsman; he was ordained a priest only in 1901, already at the age of 43, for the diocese of Viviers, at the request of his spiritual superiors, who saw in this a necessary instrument for the mission he was planning.

Still in 1901 he left for the Algerian Sahara, settling first at Beni Abbès, near the Moroccan border, and then, from 1905, at Tamanrasset, in the Hoggar (Ahaggar) massif, among the Muslim Tuareg—one of the most isolated places then accessible to a European. There Foucauld did not seek to convert anyone through direct preaching: he proposed what he called an "apostolate of goodness," a silent and fraternal presence, open to all without distinction of religion, welcoming travelers, caring for the sick in times of famine and epidemic, and devoting himself to scholarly work recording the Tuareg language and poetry, which resulted in an extensive four-volume Tuareg-French dictionary and a collection of poems, still a reference today for Berber studies. He defined himself as a "universal brother," ready to be a brother to every human being, Christian or not, and even drafted statutes for a future religious "Fraternity" that he never saw born in his lifetime—he did not have a single direct disciple during the fifteen years he spent in the desert.

On December 1, 1916, in the midst of the First World War and armed uprisings against French colonial rule in the Sahara, his hermitage at Tamanrasset was surrounded by a group of raiders linked to the Senussi brotherhood; Foucauld was shot dead outside his house, an episode whose exact circumstances are still debated today. His memory, however, was not erased: the biographer René Bazin published in 1921 a life of Foucauld, "explorer in Morocco, hermit in the Sahara Desert," which circulated widely and awakened vocations, and the scholar Louis Massignon helped preserve his spiritual writings. From these writings arose several congregations that recognize themselves as his "spiritual family": the Little Brothers of Jesus, whose first community settled at El Abiodh Sidi Cheikh, in southern Oran (Algeria), on September 8, 1933, under the direction of René Voillaume, and the Little Sisters of Jesus, founded in September 1939 at Touggourt, in Algeria, by Madeleine Hutin (Sister Magdeleine of Jesus), among other religious communities and lay associations throughout the world, united by the spirituality of hidden life, radical poverty, and universal fraternity. Declared Venerable in 2001 by John Paul II, beatified by Pope Benedict XVI on November 13, 2005, Charles de Foucauld was canonized by Pope Francis on May 15, 2022.

itens.resumo: Spanish Franciscan friar who founded nine of the missions that gave rise to important cities in California; today a figure critically reassessed by part of the historiography with regard to his treatment of Indigenous peoples.
itens.corpo:
Miquel Josep Serra i Ferrer was born on November 24, 1713, in Petra, on the island of Majorca, the son of humble farmers. He entered the Franciscan Order in 1730, taking the name Junípero in honor of one of the first companions of Saint Francis of Assisi, and he excelled in his studies to the point of becoming a professor of philosophy at the Lullian University of Palma before he was even thirty, as well as a preacher known throughout the island. Despite a promising academic career, he asked to be sent as a missionary to the Americas, sailing in 1749 for Mexico; on the overland journey between Veracruz and Mexico City he insisted on continuing on foot, despite an insect bite that infected his leg and would leave him lame and in pain for the rest of his life.

For almost nine years, Serra worked as a missionary among the Indigenous Pame people in the mountainous region of the Sierra Gorda, north of Mexico City, learning their language and supervising the construction of stone churches that still stand today. After a period as a professor and itinerant preacher in various regions of Mexico, his life changed course in 1767, when King Charles III of Spain ordered the expulsion of the Jesuits from all Spanish domains, leaving control of the missions of Baja California vacant; the Franciscans of the College of San Fernando, among them Serra, were called to take them over.

Already 55 years old, in 1769 Serra joined the land and sea expedition organized by Governor Gaspar de Portolá to occupy and evangelize Alta California, a territory then coveted by Spain in the face of the Russian and British advance along the North Pacific. On July 16, 1769, he founded the first of the missions, San Diego de Alcalá, and the following year, 1770, Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo, which would become his base and main residence and where he would be buried. Over the next fifteen years, despite his ever-wounded leg and walking with the support of a staff, he traveled on foot along the so-called El Camino Real along the California coast, founding in all nine of the eventual 21 missions of the region — among them those that gave rise to the present-day cities of San Diego, San Francisco (a mission founded in 1776, the same year as the independence of the United States), San Gabriel, San Luis Obispo, San Juan Capistrano, Santa Clara and San Buenaventura.

Each mission functioned as an agricultural, religious and productive center where local Indigenous populations — such as the Kumeyaay, the Chumash and the Ohlone — were catechized, baptized and incorporated into work on the land, in livestock raising and in artisan trades, under a communal way of life strictly regulated by the friars. Serra saw in this system a project of Christian protection and civilization of the native peoples in the face of Spanish military and civil colonization, and he even traveled to Mexico City to obtain from the viceroy a document — informally known as the "bill of rights for the Indians" — that limited abuses by soldiers against the Indigenous population of the missions.

Serra died on August 28, 1784, at Mission Carmelo, where he was buried beneath the altar of the church; it is estimated that, despite his age and frail health, he traveled on foot more than 24,000 kilometers over the course of his missionary life in America. Beatified by Pope John Paul II on September 25, 1988, he was canonized by Pope Francis on September 23, 2015, in Washington, D.C. — the first canonization held on United States soil —, in a gesture that also sought to value the Hispanic presence in the history of North American Catholicism.

The canonization, however, rekindled a historical controversy that had already existed for decades: historians, anthropologists and leaders of California Indigenous peoples document that the mission system, despite its evangelizing intentions, also imposed forced labor, corporal punishment, confinement that prevented baptized neophytes from fleeing, destruction of native cultural and religious practices, and sanitary conditions that, combined with epidemics of diseases brought by the Europeans, contributed to a severe demographic collapse among the native populations of the region in the Spanish and later Mexican period. This debate intensified publicly from 2015 onward and, in 2020, led to the toppling of several statues of Serra in the United States; the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops and Franciscans connected with the missions acknowledge the need to face this part of history honestly, while at the same time pointing to sources and testimonies that describe Serra personally as a defender of more humane treatment of the Indigenous people against the abuses of civil and military authorities of the time — a debate that the Church now considers a necessary, and still open, part of the historical evaluation of his work.

itens.resumo: A congregation with an exclusively missionary vocation, founded in the Netherlands by Saint Arnold Janssen, now present in dozens of mission countries.
itens.corpo:
The Society of the Divine Word (Societas Verbi Divini, SVD) was founded on September 8, 1875, in Steyl, a small town in the Netherlands near the German border, by Father Arnold Janssen. A German diocesan priest born in 1837, Janssen had for years been growing in the conviction that Catholic Germany needed a missionary institute of its own — unlike France, Italy or Spain, the country had no congregation dedicated specifically to sending missionaries ad gentes — but he was prevented from founding one on German soil by the Kulturkampf, the anti-Catholic policy pursued by Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, which closed seminaries, expelled religious orders and persecuted the clergy faithful to Rome. That is why Janssen established his foundation across the border, in a small house acquired in Steyl with the support of German bishops sympathetic to the project.

Aware of the importance of the media for attracting vocations and resources, Janssen opened a small printing press in the missionary house itself just a few months after the foundation, publishing the periodical Kleiner Herz-Jesu-Bote ("Little Messenger of the Sacred Heart") as a means of publicity and of gathering support — an editorial initiative that would grow greatly in the following decades and become a trademark of the congregation's work. The first two missionaries trained in Steyl, among them the future saint Joseph Freinademetz, left for China on March 2, 1879, only four years after the foundation, beginning the evangelizing work that would become the congregation's reason for being; the Society's definitive pontifical approval would come in 1901.

The Congregation of the Divine Word arrived in Brazil in 1895, settling above all in Rio Grande do Sul and later expanding into other regions of the country, where today it maintains parishes, seminaries, universities (such as the Uniarnaldo network) and media outlets, celebrating more than 125 years of missionary presence in Brazil. Throughout the twentieth century the SVD spread across all continents, with a strong presence also in Asia (Indonesia, the Philippines, India), Oceania and Africa, and today it is the largest men's congregation dedicated specifically to mission ad gentes and one of the largest men's congregations in the Catholic Church in number of members, gathering more than six thousand religious — priests and brothers — spread across about 80 countries on all continents, ahead even of other men's congregations that are older and larger in absolute numbers, but without the exclusively missionary profile of the Society of the Divine Word.

The spirituality of the Society of the Divine Word is centered on the Word of God — the "Word" (Logos) of the prologue of the Gospel of John, who became flesh and dwelt among us — understood as the source and model of all missionary activity: just as the Word became incarnate in a concrete culture and language, the Divine Word missionary is called to become deeply inserted into the cultures where he works. The congregation also has a strong devotion to the Most Holy Trinity, understood as a communion of love from which the impulse of every evangelizing mission springs, and to the Holy Spirit as the force that drives the Church out of itself.

Arnold Janssen did not limit himself to founding the missionary priests and brothers: in 1889 he also founded, with the collaboration of Hendrina Stollenwerk, the Holy Spirit Missionary Sisters, a women's branch devoted to the same spirituality, and later a contemplative branch, the Holy Spirit Adoration Sisters, dedicated to prayer for the missions. Janssen died in Steyl on January 15, 1909, without seeing the worldwide reach his work would attain; he was beatified in 1975 and canonized by Pope John Paul II on October 5, 2003, together with Joseph Freinademetz, his first missionary sent to China.

The printing press founded by Janssen in Steyl, which had begun modestly as a means of publicity and financial support for the young congregation, grew over the following decades until it became one of the largest German-language Catholic publishers dedicated to missionary topics, publishing magazines and ethnographic and linguistic studies produced by SVD missionaries themselves in their territories of work — a tradition of scientific research allied with evangelization that earned the congregation academic recognition in fields such as anthropology and missionary linguistics, especially through the scientific journal Anthropos, founded in 1906 by the Austrian Divine Word priest Wilhelm Schmidt and still today an international reference in ethnology and linguistics.

itens.resumo: A missionary institute founded in Turin by Saint Giuseppe Allamano, dedicated above all to the evangelization of countries in East Africa.
itens.corpo:
Giuseppe Allamano was born on January 21, 1851, in Castelnuovo d'Asti (now Castelnuovo Don Bosco), in Italy's Piedmont region — the same small hometown as Saint John Bosco, to whom he was a close relative — and he was the maternal nephew of Saint Joseph Cafasso, the famous "spiritual father of the Turin clergy." Ordained a priest in 1873, Allamano devoted himself above all to priestly formation and, beginning in 1880, became rector of the Shrine of the Consolata in Turin, an important center of Marian devotion in the city, a post he would hold for 46 years, until his death, raising the shrine to a new level of spiritual life and pilgrimage.

From his youth he had nurtured the dream of creating a missionary institute from Turin, motivated both by the example of Don Bosco and Cafasso and by the then-growing call for missionaries to Africa, newly "opened" to European presence. He founded the Consolata Missions Institute on January 29, 1901, with the approval of the Archbishop of Turin, and sent the first four missionaries — two priests and two brothers — to British Kenya in May 1902, establishing the first Consolata mission at Tuthu, in the Kenyan interior, soon followed by other stations in the region of Nyeri and Mount Kenya. Allamano never traveled to Africa himself, remaining in Turin as formator and spiritual director at a distance for his missionaries, with whom he kept up an intense correspondence.

His spiritual pedagogy was summed up in a phrase that became the institute's motto: missionaries should be "saints before being missionaries," that is, the soundness of spiritual life and human formation should precede and ground any concrete apostolic action — Allamano feared hasty missionaries, technically competent but spiritually shallow. He asked his religious to be "persevering, united and enlightened" in proclaiming the Kingdom of God, and he closely associated evangelization with human development, directing his missionaries also to care for the health, education and material development of the communities where they worked, within a spirituality centered on the Trinity and marked by a strong Marian devotion, inherited from his life at the shrine.

In 1910, Allamano founded the women's branch of the institute, the Consolata Missionary Sisters, extending the reach of the work to areas of community life and health care where the presence of women religious proved indispensable. From the Kenyan base, the two Consolata institutes expanded throughout the twentieth century to Ethiopia (from 1913, though with interruptions due to political conflicts), Tanzania, Somalia and, already in the 1920s, Mozambique; later, on June 14, 1948, a group of Consolata missionaries led by José Nepote Fus arrived in Boa Vista, then the capital of the Federal Territory of Rio Branco, to replace the Benedictine monks who had worked there and to take charge of the evangelization of what would become Roraima — the beginning of an Amazonian presence that continues to this day. Beginning in 1971, the Consolata missionaries in Roraima made the so-called "option for the indigenous peoples," going to live within the communities and malocas themselves, rather than working from farms and colonization centers as before, redirecting their work toward a pastoral approach closer to indigenous culture and autonomy. Today the Consolata Missionary Fathers and Sisters are present in more than thirty countries on four continents.

Allamano died in Turin on February 16, 1926, without ever having seen in person the Africa for which he spent his life forming missionaries to evangelize. He was beatified by Pope John Paul II on October 7, 1990, and canonized by Pope Francis on October 20, 2024, World Mission Day, after the recognition of a miracle that took place in the Brazilian Amazon, where the Consolata Missionaries have worked since 1948, above all among indigenous peoples of Roraima such as those of the Raposa Serra do Sol Indigenous Land and the Yanomami: on February 7, 1996, the first day of a novena to Allamano, who was then still a blessed, the Yanomami man Sorino was attacked by a jaguar that split open his skull, and, taken to the hospital in Boa Vista under the care and constant prayer of Consolata sisters, he recovered completely within a few months — a healing that the Church recognized as miraculous after a diocesan process concluded in 2021 and the final approval of the competent Roman dicastery in May 2024.

itens.resumo: A society of apostolic life that brings together diocesan secular priests dedicated exclusively to the mission ad gentes, born from the merger of two Italian missionary institutes.
itens.corpo:
PIME has its origin in the Lombard Seminary for Foreign Missions, established on July 30, 1850 in the family home of Father Angelo Ramazzotti, in Saronno, in Lombardy, and formally founded on December 1 of the same year, with the support of the other bishops of the region. Ramazzotti was born in Milan on August 3, 1800, earned a law degree at the University of Pavia in 1823, and was ordained a priest in 1829, joining the Missionary Oblates of Rho on the same day. A few months after founding the Lombard seminary, in September 1850, he was consecrated Bishop of Pavia, a diocese he governed until 1858, when he was appointed Patriarch of Venice, a post he held until his death in 1861 — thus following from a distance, and already as a bishop, the first years of the institute he had founded. He conceived the new institute at the request of Pope Pius IX, relying on the principle, innovative at the time, that spreading the Gospel among non-Christian peoples was the shared responsibility of all dioceses, and not the exclusive task of centralized religious orders — hence the model of a society of apostolic life, bringing together diocesan secular priests who committed themselves permanently and exclusively to the mission ad gentes, without the religious vows proper to an order, but with a promise of perseverance in the society.

The institute was the first born on Italian soil dedicated entirely to foreign missions, and its first missionaries departed as early as 1852 for the vicariate of Central Bengal, in India, followed in the following decades by others to Burma, Hong Kong, and other regions of Asia then difficult for European missionaries to access. As early as April 1872 the institute launched its own periodical, initially named Le Missioni Cattoliche and renamed Mondo e Missione in 1969, a publication that has remained in uninterrupted circulation to this day and is considered the oldest Italian missionary magazine still active. In parallel, in Rome, another institute with a similar profile was founded in 1871 on the initiative of the priest Pietro Avanzini, the Pontifical Roman Seminary of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, dedicated to the formation of missionaries chiefly for China; in 1926, Pope Pius XI, by means of the motu proprio Cum missionalium opera, formally united the two institutes, giving rise to the present Pontifical Institute for Foreign Missions, with headquarters in Milan and Rome.

Throughout the twentieth century, PIME expanded its presence chiefly in Asia (India, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Hong Kong, the Philippines, Japan, Papua New Guinea), but also in Africa (Guinea-Bissau, Ivory Coast, Cameroon, Mozambique) and in the Americas. It arrived in Brazil in 1946, at the invitation and with the encouragement of Pope Pius XII, devoting itself chiefly to the evangelization of riverside and Indigenous populations of the Amazon; it established missionary bases in Manaus, Macapá and São Paulo, and in 2020 completed 170 years since its founding, with decades of uninterrupted work in the Amazon.

PIME's history is also marked by martyrdom: among its members officially recognized by the Church are Father Alberico Crescitelli, killed in China in 1900 during the Boxer Rebellion and canonized in 2000 among the Chinese martyrs, Blessed John Baptist Mazzucconi, killed in Oceania in 1855, and Blessed Mario Vergara, killed in Burma in 1950, as well as confessors of the faith who were beatified, such as Paolo Manna, former superior general of the institute and theorist of twentieth-century missionary spirituality, and Clemente Vismara, a missionary in Burma for more than 65 years.

As a society of apostolic life, PIME is distinct both from a religious order and from an ordinary diocese: its members remain incardinated in the society (not in a diocese of origin), live in community, and act under the direction of a superior general elected periodically at a general chapter, working in close collaboration with the Congregation (today Dicastery) for the Evangelization of Peoples and with the local Churches in which they are placed. More than 170 years after its founding, the institute today brings together about 425 priests and brothers spread across about 19 countries on four continents, and over its history it has sent more than two thousand missionaries abroad; in May 2019 and again in recent years, popes have received in audience the participants of PIME's general chapter, reaffirming the institute's role in the so-called missionary renewal of the Church in the twenty-first century.

itens.resumo: Missionary settlements organized by Jesuits among the Guaraní peoples in colonial South America, combining evangelization, protection against enslavement, and a distinct social organization.
itens.corpo:
Beginning in the early seventeenth century, on the initiative of a group of Jesuits led by the provincial Diego de Torres Bollo, the Society of Jesus began to organize, in the basins of the Paraná, Paraguay and Uruguay rivers, missionary settlements called "reductions" — from the Latin reductio ad unum, "to gather in one place" — Guaraní populations that lived scattered in small groups throughout the forest, bringing them into fixed settlements where they could receive religious instruction, artistic training and trades, and live under their own laws and free labor, in contrast to the encomienda system and the enslavement practiced by the surrounding colonizers. At the height of the system, between 1730 and 1750, there existed the so-called "Thirty Peoples" of the Missions, bringing together a population estimated at about 145,000 Guaraní Indigenous people.

Each reduction was organized around a large central plaza, with the church — normally the most monumental building of the settlement — on one side, and on the other the cemetery, the priests' residence, workshops, common storehouses, a school and, around them, the houses of the Guaraní families arranged in regular blocks; gardens, communal fields and family subsistence plots (called abambaé and tupambaé) ensured both the sustenance of the families and the surplus traded by the reduction as a whole, above all yerba mate, cotton and cattle. The daily government of each settlement fell to a cabildo (town council) on the Spanish model, but made up and presided over by Indigenous leaders — caciques and other elected Guaraní — with the Jesuit priests, normally only two or three per reduction, acting as spiritual and administrative advisers, never as direct political authority.

The Spanish Jesuit Antonio Ruiz de Montoya, one of the central figures in the history of the reductions, worked between 1612 and 1631 chiefly in the region of Guairá (today's territory of Paraná in Brazil and of Paraguay), even leading, in 1631, a dramatic river migration of thousands of Guaraní downstream to escape attacks by bandeirantes from São Paulo, hunters of slaves; he left a record of this experience in the chronicle Spiritual Conquest (1639), an essential primary source for the history of the period, and he also compiled one of the first dictionaries and grammars of the Guaraní language.

The reductions also became a center of artistic and musical production of great originality, today called "missionary Baroque" or "Guaraní Baroque": under the guidance of priests trained in European music, painting, sculpture and architecture, Guaraní craftsmen developed workshops for carving, sacred painting, bell founding and, above all, a vocal and instrumental musical tradition (with regular orchestras and choirs in each settlement) that fused European techniques with Indigenous sensibilities and materials — a heritage of scores and instruments that partially survives to this day and has been the object of musicological recovery in recent decades.

The system, however, also depended on the military protection organized by the Guaraní of the reductions themselves, authorized by the Spanish crown to arm and train themselves against the constant attacks of Portuguese bandeirantes coming from São Paulo in search of slave labor — which made the reductions, paradoxically, one of the best-organized military forces in the River Plate region in the seventeenth century. This balance was broken by the Treaty of Madrid of 1750, by which Spain and Portugal exchanged territories: seven eastern reductions (the "Seven Peoples of the Missions") were to be handed over to the Portuguese crown in exchange for Colônia do Sacramento, which led to the Guaraní armed resistance known as the Guaraní War (1753-1756), in which Luso-Spanish troops militarily crushed the Indigenous populations, killing more than 1,500 people in the decisive battle of Caibaté in 1756.

The definitive collapse of the system came with the expulsion of the Jesuits from the dominions of Portugal in 1759, and of Spain in 1767, by decision of the respective absolutist monarchs, who saw in the reductions an excessive parallel power; without the Jesuits, the reductions were progressively abandoned, plundered and absorbed by other forms of colonization, and their Indigenous population dispersed or was assimilated. Today the ruins of several of these reductions — such as São Miguel das Missões in Brazil, San Ignacio Miní in Argentina, and Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangué in Paraguay — are recognized as UNESCO World Heritage Sites and remain studied as one of the most original, and still debated, experiments in social organization and evangelization in colonial American history.

itens.resumo: A period of rapid expansion and then violent persecution of Christianity in Japan, between the arrival of Saint Francis Xavier in 1549 and the country's near-total isolation in the seventeenth century.
itens.corpo:
A term coined by the British historian Charles Boxer in his classic book The Christian Century in Japan (1951), the "Christian Century" designates the period of roughly one hundred years that runs from the arrival of Francis Xavier in Japan in August 1549 to the virtual eradication of visible Christianity in the archipelago in the mid-seventeenth century. The Japanese called the missionaries and their converts kirishitan, a local transliteration of the Portuguese word "cristão" (Christian), and Christianity itself kirishitan-shū ("Christian sect"), a term that Japanese historiography still uses today to designate this whole chapter of the country's religious history.

After Xavier left Japan in 1551, Jesuits such as Cosme de Torres and, later, the influential Alessandro Valignano continued the mission, increasingly adopting the method of cultural adaptation begun by Xavier: deep study of the Japanese language and etiquette, the use of garments similar to those of Buddhist monks and, later, of the literati, and careful outreach to the local feudal lords (daimyos), several of whom converted and favored evangelization in their domains. The most notable case was Ōmura Sumitada, the first Christian daimyo, who in 1580 ceded to the Jesuits the small fishing port of Nagasaki, a city that would become the main Christian and commercial center of Japan. Spanish Franciscans, Dominicans and Augustinians, coming from the Philippines, joined the mission from the 1590s onward, broadening its evangelizing reach but also generating rivalries among the orders that would weigh on Japanese policy toward Christianity.

The growth was remarkable: according to estimates of the time, the Japanese Christian community came to exceed between 300,000 and 500,000 faithful around 1600, a significant figure for a total population of the archipelago then of about twenty million, concentrated above all on the island of Kyushu. A diocese of its own, with its seat in Funai (Bungo), was erected in 1588, and there came to be a seminary and a Jesuit college training local clergy. In 1582 four young Japanese Christian nobles were sent by Valignano on an embassy to Europe, the so-called "Tensho Mission," which visited Lisbon, Madrid and Rome and was received by Pope Gregory XIII, a symbolic episode of how promising and lasting the Japanese mission then seemed.

The reversal began in 1587, when the unifying regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi, fearing that the loyalty of the Christian daimyos and the presence of the Iberian powers could threaten his newly consolidated authority, issued an edict expelling the priests (bateren tsuihō-rei), although he did not apply it systematically at once. The persecution became bloody in 1597, when Hideyoshi ordered the crucifixion of 26 Christians (Franciscans, Jesuits and Japanese laypeople) on Nishizaka hill in Nagasaki, an episode that would become the best-known symbol of Japanese Christian martyrdom. After Hideyoshi's death (1598) and the rise of Tokugawa Ieyasu as the new shogun, the initial tolerance gave way, from 1612-1614, to a total prohibition: the edict of 1614 banned Christianity from the entire territory, formally expelled all religious orders and ordered the destruction of churches, although several missionaries and catechists remained clandestinely for years.

The repression intensified in the following decades under Ieyasu's successors, including the systematic use of the fumie (stepping on sacred images to prove apostasy) as a test of loyalty, culminating in the violent Shimabara Rebellion (1637-1638), a peasant uprising with a strong Christian component harshly crushed by the shogunate, which killed tens of thousands of people and sealed the end of any tolerance. Japan then adopted the policy of near-total isolation known as sakoku (1639-1853), closing the country to practically all Western contact, except for a restricted Dutch trading post on the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki, and making the practice of Christianity a capital crime for more than two centuries.

Without clergy, without institutional contact with Rome and under constant risk of discovery and execution, entire communities of Christians came to live in complete clandestinity, adapting prayers, sacraments and lay leadership to a format that could be transmitted secretly from generation to generation: the so-called kakure kirishitan ("hidden Christians"). These communities came to light publicly only after Japan reopened to the West in the mid-nineteenth century, when, in 1865, a group of peasants from Urakami, near Nagasaki, revealed their faith to a newly arrived French priest at the then-new Ōura Church, an episode known as the "discovery of the Christians" (Kirishitan Hakken), which surprised the Catholic world by showing that the faith had survived, without priests, for more than two centuries of systematic persecution.

itens.resumo: A group of young Christians from the court of the kingdom of Buganda, executed between 1885 and 1887 for refusing to renounce their faith; canonized in 1964 as witnesses to the evangelization of Africa.
itens.corpo:
The Catholic evangelization of the kingdom of Buganda, in the interior of present-day Uganda, began in 1879 with the arrival of the first White Fathers (Missionaries of Africa), founded by Charles Lavigerie, who found in the court of the kabaka (king) Mutesa I an atmosphere of religious curiosity, already contested as well by Anglican Protestant missionaries and by Muslim traders from the Swahili coast. After the death of Mutesa I in 1884, his adolescent son Mwanga II came to the throne, a young man of unstable and violent temperament, who saw in the Christian pages of his court — many of whom refused to satisfy his sexual demands upon the young men of the royal court — both a challenge to his authority and a political threat, because of the loyalty many of them gave to a foreign faith rather than to the kabaka himself.

The persecution began formally on November 15, 1885, when Mwanga ordered the beheading of Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe, chief steward of the court and a fervent Catholic who had publicly rebuked the king for his abuses — becoming the first martyr of the group. After the death of Mukasa, the leadership of the court's Christian community fell to Charles Lwanga, head of the royal pages, who began to protect the young Christians in secret, to baptize catechumens in haste in the face of imminent danger, and to strengthen the group in the faith, knowing that the persecution could intensify at any moment.

In May 1886, upon discovering that several pages had rejected his advances and remained faithful to Christian instruction, Mwanga gathered the court and demanded that all Christians present themselves separately from the others; those who identified themselves as Catholics or Anglicans were condemned to death. On June 3, 1886, Charles Lwanga and twelve Catholic companions were taken to Namugongo, about forty kilometers from the royal palace at Munyonyo — a journey that local tradition describes as a veritable Way of the Cross, marked by beatings and further attempts to make them renounce the faith — and there they were wrapped in reed mats and burned alive on a great collective pyre; among them was Kizito, the youngest of the group, only thirteen or fourteen years old. In the same period, Anglican Christians of the court were likewise executed by order of Mwanga, uniting Catholics and Protestants in a single episode of persecution.

In all, between January 31, 1885 and January 27, 1887, forty-five Christians of the court of Buganda were put to death by order of Mwanga II — twenty-two Catholics and twenty-three Anglicans —, most of them very young, between thirteen and thirty years old, many serving as pages or servants close to the king. Among the twenty-two canonized Catholics are, besides Charles Lwanga and Joseph Mukasa, names such as Matthias Mulumba Kalemba, a local chief older than the others, executed with refined cruelty on May 30, 1886; Andrew Kaggwa, in charge of music at the royal court; and Pontian Ngondwe, one of the royal guards — a group that thus brought together both young pages and adult men of different roles in the structure of the court of Buganda. Paradoxically, the persecution did not halt the spread of Christianity in the region: in the following decades the Christian faith grew rapidly in Uganda, and the accounts of the martyrdom, transmitted orally and later in writing by the white missionaries, quickly became part of Ugandan Catholic identity.

The twenty-two Catholic martyrs were beatified by Pope Benedict XV in 1920, and Pius XI declared Charles Lwanga, in 1934, patron of African Catholic youth. The canonization of the whole group was celebrated by Pope Paul VI on October 18, 1964, during a session of the Second Vatican Council — the first canonization of modern African saints, and a gesture of strong symbolic significance at a time when several African countries were attaining political independence. On July 29, 1969, Paul VI traveled in person to Kampala to consecrate the high altar of the shrine built at Namugongo — constructed with a circular architecture inspired by the traditional African hut and supported by twenty-two pillars in memory of the Catholic martyrs —, on what became the first journey of a pope to the African continent; the shrine and the date of June 3, now a national holiday in Uganda, receive each year hundreds of thousands of pilgrims from all over East Africa.

itens.resumo: A group of three Jesuits, six Franciscans, and seventeen lay Christians — among them Saint Philip of Jesus, the first saint born in Mexico — crucified at Nagasaki in 1597, the first great mass martyrdom of Christianity in Japan.
itens.corpo:
The martyrdom of the 26 Martyrs of Japan arose from a combination of political and religious factors that had been accumulating since the late 1580s. Christianity had arrived in the archipelago in 1549, when Francis Xavier, Cosme de Torres, and Juan Fernández landed at Kagoshima, and for decades the Jesuit mission enjoyed the favor of powerful men, among them Oda Nobunaga, who saw in the foreign religious a means of weakening the Buddhist sects and of facilitating trade with Portugal and Spain. His successor, the unifying regent Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who took a more conservative stance toward outside influences, had already issued in 1587 the first edict banning Christianity and expelling the Jesuit missionaries, motivated by the fear that the loyalty of converted daimyos and the presence of Iberian powers on the Japanese coast would threaten his newly won authority; the edict, however, was not applied systematically for almost a decade.

The situation deteriorated in 1596, when the shipwreck of the Spanish galleon San Felipe on the Japanese coast led to rumors — attributed to an indiscreet remark by a Spanish pilot — that Catholic missionaries were preparing the ground for a future Spanish military conquest of Japan, as Spain had done in the Philippines. In response, Hideyoshi ordered the arrest of missionaries and Japanese Christians in Kyoto and Osaka as a show of force.

Twenty-four people were initially arrested — six Franciscan friars, among them the mission superior, Pedro Bautista, the Spaniard Francisco Blanco, and Gonçalo Garcia, born in 1556 in Vasai (Bassein), in Portuguese India, the son of a Portuguese father and an Indian mother, as well as the novice Felipe de las Casas, born in Mexico City in 1572 (Saint Philip of Jesus, the first saint born in the territory that is now Mexico); three Japanese Jesuits (Father Paul Miki and Brothers John Soan de Goto and James Kisai); and fifteen lay people connected to the Franciscan Third Order — catechists and servants of the missions, fourteen Japanese and one Korean — among them two boys, Louis Ibaraki and Anthony of Nagasaki. While still in Kyoto, by order of Hideyoshi himself, part of their left ear was cut off as a mark of infamy, and they were forced to parade publicly through several Japanese cities during a month-long forced march toward Nagasaki, the country's main Christian center, where the execution was to serve as a public example; two lay Christians who accompanied the group along the way, offering them assistance, were also arrested and added to the group, bringing the total to twenty-six.

On February 5, 1597, the twenty-six were taken to the hill of Nishizaka, on the outskirts of Nagasaki, and tied and chained to wooden crosses erected side by side; following a method used in Japan at the time, each was killed with crossed spear thrusts to the chest, delivered by soldiers positioned on both sides of the cross, and not by nails or asphyxiation as in traditional Roman crucifixion. Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit of about 33 years of age, used his last moments to preach from his own cross to the assembled crowd, declaring himself Japanese and a religious of the Society of Jesus, forgiving his executioners, and affirming his joy at dying for the faith he had freely chosen — a speech that witnesses present recorded and that became the most famous account of the episode.

News of the martyrdom spread quickly through Asia and Europe by way of the annual letters of the Jesuits and Franciscan accounts, becoming one of the most widely publicized episodes in the missionary history of the Far East in the sixteenth century, both for the number of victims and for the presence of children and of religious of different orders put to death side by side. The group was beatified by Pope Urban VIII on September 14, 1627 — three of them, the Jesuits, had their beatification confirmed in 1629 — and canonized by Pope Pius IX on June 8, 1862, making Paul Miki the first native Japanese religious raised to sainthood by the Catholic Church.

The 26 Martyrs of Japan are celebrated liturgically on February 6 and are regarded, together with the martyrs of Nagasaki of later generations, as patrons of Japan; in 1962, on the centenary of their canonization, a bronze monument with the twenty-six figures, the work of the sculptor Yasutake Funakoshi, was erected on the top of the Nishizaka hill, beside a museum dedicated to the memory of the Japanese Christian martyrs, which remains today one of the main Catholic pilgrimage sites in the country. This 1597 group must not be confused with two other great groups of Japanese martyrs recognized later by the Church: the 205 Martyrs of Japan, beatified by Pope Pius IX on July 7, 1867, who died between 1617 and 1632 already under the systematic persecution of the Tokugawa shogunate, and the 188 Martyrs of Japan, beatified on November 24, 2008 — both later groups, evidence that the persecution of Japanese Christianity, begun with the martyrdom at Nishizaka, would extend for decades with growing intensity until the near-total closing of the country to the West.

itens.titulo: Ad Gentes (Conciliar Decree on the Mission Activity of the Church)
itens.resumo: Decree of the Second Vatican Council that reaffirms the intrinsically missionary nature of the Church and lays the foundations of the modern theology of mission.
itens.corpo:
The decree Ad Gentes ("To the Nations", from the opening words of the Latin text) was one of the last documents promulgated by the Second Vatican Council. It was approved by a vote of 2,394 in favor to only five against and signed by Pope Paul VI on December 7, 1965, the eve of the Council's solemn closing. Its final drafting was preceded by a troubled process: a first schema presented in 1962 was judged too weak and sent back for revision, and only in the fourth and last session of the Council, under the coordination of a commission that included experts such as the then young theologian Joseph Ratzinger, did the text acquire the theological density that would make it a lasting reference on the missionary nature of the Church.

Until the Council, the Roman governance of missionary activity belonged chiefly to the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Propaganda Fide), established in 1622 by Pope Gregory XV, the same year in which Gregory XV canonized Francis Xavier, as a centralized body to coordinate and oversee all evangelization in non-Christian territories. Ad Gentes did not abolish this administrative structure (today the Dicastery for Evangelization), but it provided it, more than three centuries later, with a systematic theological foundation that it had previously lacked.

The theological core of the document is already found in the first paragraph: the Church is "missionary by her very nature" ("Ecclesia... natura sua missionaria est"), since she has her origin in the mission of the Son and the Holy Spirit sent by the Father, according to God's plan to gather together all humanity scattered by sin. This affirmation was a turning point in relation to earlier formulations that treated mission as one activity among others of the Church, delegated to specialists or to specific religious orders: for the Council, missionary activity ad gentes flows directly from the Church's identity as the "universal sacrament of salvation", the sign and instrument of intimate union with God and of the unity of the whole human race.

The decree is structured in six chapters. The first presents the doctrinal principles, rooting mission in the very Trinitarian life of God and in Christ's mandate to the apostles ("Go therefore and make disciples of all nations"); the second, "Missionary Work Itself", descends to the concrete: the witness of Christian life, the preaching and gathering together of the People of God, the formation of the Christian community, and the activity of charity that must accompany every evangelizing proclamation. The following chapters deal with the particular churches that must be born and mature in mission territory until they become fully responsible for themselves (chapter III), with missionaries themselves, their vocation and their spiritual and technical formation (chapter IV), with the organization of missionary activity, including the role of Roman dicasteries and the cooperation between bishops and religious institutes (chapter V), and finally with the cooperation of the whole Church in mission: bishops, priests, religious and, explicitly and in a way then relatively new for a conciliar document, the laity, called to collaborate actively in the evangelization of peoples (chapter VI).

Among the most discussed statements of the document, in number 11, is the recognition that "seeds of the Word" (semina Verbi) and elements of truth and grace may be present in the religious and cultural traditions of peoples not yet evangelized. This idea, without diluting the necessity of the explicit proclamation of Christ, opened the way in the following decades to a more positive appreciation of interreligious dialogue and inculturation. The decree also insists that missionary activity must respect people's freedom of conscience and adapt itself, without losing doctrinal fidelity, to the authentic cultural values of each people, a reflection that dialogues directly with the historical practice of missionaries such as Matteo Ricci or José de Anchieta, although without naming them.

The reception of Ad Gentes over the following decades was ambiguous: part of the post-conciliar reflection, also influenced by the constitution Gaudium et Spes and by the emphasis on interreligious dialogue, led some theologians to relativize the urgency of explicit missionary activity ad gentes. It was partly to reaffirm this urgency, twenty-five years later, that Pope John Paul II published in 1990 the encyclical Redemptoris Missio, which presents itself explicitly as an update and reaffirmation of the principles of Ad Gentes in the face of a world that had changed profoundly since the Council. To this day, Ad Gentes remains the official reference document of the Catholic Church on the theological foundations, methods and institutional organization of missionary activity ad gentes.

itens.resumo: Encyclical of Saint John Paul II on the permanent validity of the Church's missionary mandate, published 25 years after the conciliar decree Ad Gentes.
itens.corpo:
Published on December 7, 1990 — a date deliberately chosen to coincide with the twenty-fifth anniversary of the conciliar decree Ad Gentes and the fifteenth of Paul VI's apostolic exhortation Evangelii Nuntiandi —, the encyclical Redemptoris Missio ("The Mission of the Redeemer"), the eighth of John Paul II's pontificate, bears the subtitle "on the permanent validity of the Church's missionary mandate" and arose from a concrete pastoral concern of the Pope: the perception that, within the Church herself, a certain discouragement or relativization was growing regarding the urgency of evangelizing peoples who did not yet know Christ, fed by theological currents that valued interreligious dialogue to the point of questioning whether the explicit proclamation of the Gospel was still necessary or even legitimate in a pluralistic world.

The document opens by reaffirming that the mission of Christ the Redeemer, entrusted by Him to the Church, "is still very far from completion": as the second Christian millennium draws to a close, John Paul II argues, an overall view of the human race shows that world evangelization is still only beginning, and that it would be a mistake to consider the missionary task as completed or dispensable. One of the encyclical's most frequently cited and lasting contributions is the clear distinction between three different pastoral situations that the Church faces simultaneously: the mission ad gentes properly so called, directed to peoples, human groups and sociocultural contexts where Christ and his Gospel are not yet known or where there are no ecclesial communities sufficiently mature to live and proclaim the faith by themselves; ordinary pastoral care, carried out among Christian communities already endowed with solid and adequate ecclesial structures; and the so-called "new evangelization", directed to groups of baptized persons who have drifted away from a living faith or never came to profess it in a personal and mature way, especially in secularized regions of long-established Christianity.

John Paul II insists that these three situations, although distinct, are neither watertight nor ranked in a simplistic way, but that the first of them — the mission ad gentes — retains a priority and an urgency that none of the others replaces, and he warns against the tendency, which he saw growing in sectors of the post-conciliar Church, to dissolve this specificity under the argument that "the whole Church is always missionary" in a generic sense. At the same time, the encyclical devotes an important chapter to the Holy Spirit as "the principal agent of the whole of the Church's mission", present and active not only in the Church but, in mysterious ways, also in the lives of persons, cultures and religions outside her — a theological foundation that the encyclical uses to value interreligious dialogue positively without, however, giving up the conviction that the fullness of revelation and salvation is found only in Jesus Christ.

The text is organized in eight chapters, with titles that summarize well its line of argument: "Jesus Christ, the Only Savior", "The Kingdom of God", "The Holy Spirit, the Principal Agent of Mission", "The Vast Horizons of the Mission Ad Gentes", "The Paths of Mission", "Leaders and Workers in the Missionary Apostolate", "Cooperation in the Missionary Apostolate" and, finally, "Missionary Spirituality" — a structure that moves from the Christological and pneumatological foundation to the more practical and spiritual dimension of the missionary sending.

Within these chapters the document also addresses the various "paths of mission" — simple witness of life, the first explicit proclamation of Christ, conversion and baptism, the formation of local ecclesial communities, the inculturation of the Gospel in different cultures, dialogue with followers of other religions, and human promotion and the integral development of peoples as an inseparable dimension of the evangelical proclamation. It also treats at length the "agents" of missionary activity — bishops, fidei donum priests, men and women religious, missionary institutes, lay people and volunteers — and the spirituality proper to the missionary, marked by docility to the Spirit, by apostolic love in the likeness of Paul, and by a holiness that the encyclical considers an indispensable prerequisite, not an accessory, of any effective evangelizing action.

Since its publication, Redemptoris Missio has become one of the most frequently cited reference texts of contemporary Catholic missiology, studied in seminaries and missionary institutes around the world and often invoked in later documents — including Pope Francis's apostolic exhortation Evangelii Gaudium (2013), which takes up and develops several of its central themes, such as the joy of proclamation, inculturation, and attention to the poor as the privileged recipients of the mission.

itens.resumo: A worldwide network of prayer and material support for the missions, begun by the French laywoman Pauline Jaricot in 1822 and now coordinated by the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples.
itens.corpo:
Pauline Marie Jaricot was born in 1799 in Lyon, France, the youngest of seven children of a prosperous family of silk merchants. Raised in a bourgeois and devout environment, at the age of seventeen she suffered the loss of her mother and went through an experience of personal conversion that led her to abandon a life of vanities and devote herself to works of charity among the poor workers of the silk factories of Lyon, whose working conditions she knew firsthand through her own family's trade. It was this contact with factory life, together with the news reaching Lyon about the urgent needs of French Catholic missionaries in China and America — many of them former seminary classmates of her brother, who had become a priest and left as a missionary — that led her to conceive an original model of support for the missions.

Beginning in 1818, Jaricot organized among the women workers of the Lyon silk factories a simple and effective system of collecting funds: each person committed to praying daily one single mystery of the rosary and to giving a small weekly sum (initially one sou), while seeking out ten other people to do the same, forming "groups of ten" that multiplied in a chain and whose combined funds supported missionaries throughout the world. This system evolved and was formalized as an association on May 3, 1822, a date recognized as the official founding of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith — considered the first organized worldwide network of prayer and material solidarity with the Catholic missions, and whose "chain" model of donors would inspire, decades later, similar practices in other charitable institutions.

Jaricot did not stop there: in 1826 she also founded the Association of the Living Rosary, dividing the rosary into fifteen (later twenty) mysteries distributed among groups of the faithful, who thus prayed the complete rosary in communion of intention, an initiative of popular spirituality that spread widely throughout France and beyond. Her personal life, however, was marked by setbacks: she invested a large part of her fortune and that of her family in a model factory project with better conditions for workers, the so-called "Rustrel Factory," which failed financially and left her in debt and humiliated in the last years of her life; she died poor and virtually forgotten in Lyon, in 1862.

In 1843, complementing Jaricot's work, the French bishop Charles de Forbin-Janson founded in Paris the Society of the Holy Childhood (today Missionary Childhood Association), intended to involve children in prayer and in modest material collaboration with children in mission countries, and later there arose the Society of Saint Peter the Apostle, dedicated specifically to supporting seminaries and to the formation of native clergy and religious in mission territories, and the Pontifical Missionary Union of Clergy and Religious, founded in Italy and aimed at the missionary animation of priests, religious brothers and sisters. In 1922, Pope Pius XI, recognizing the effectiveness and reach of these grassroots initiatives, raised the first three works to the status of "pontifical," placing them directly under the Congregation (today Dicastery) for the Evangelization of Peoples; the Missionary Union of Clergy was recognized as the fourth pontifical society in 1956 by Pope Pius XII.

Today the Pontifical Mission Societies (PMS) bring together these four branches — Propagation of the Faith, Holy Childhood, Saint Peter the Apostle and Missionary Union — organized in an international, national and diocesan structure present in practically every country in the world, functioning as the Catholic Church's main official instrument of cooperation and of material and spiritual support for missionary activity ad gentes, financing everything from the construction of churches and seminaries to social projects and the formation of pastoral workers in mission territories. In its institutional logic, this structure of cooperation goes back to the Sacred Congregation de Propaganda Fide itself, created in 1622 by Pope Gregory XV as the central body for coordinating the Catholic missions — the Pontifical Mission Societies were born, two centuries later, as the popular and voluntary arm of that same task, mobilizing ordinary faithful rather than only ecclesiastical or state resources. The cause for the beatification of Pauline Jaricot, opened at the request of Pope Pius XI as early as 1926, advanced slowly over the course of the twentieth century: declared Venerable by John XXIII in 1963, she was beatified on May 22, 2022, the year in which the Society for the Propagation of the Faith also celebrated the two hundredth anniversary of its founding.

itens.titulo: Saints Cyril and Methodius, Apostles of the Slavs
itens.resumo: Brothers from Thessalonica in the ninth century, they evangelized the Slavs of Great Moravia in the people's own language, inventing the Glagolitic alphabet. Proclaimed co-patrons of Europe in 1980.
itens.corpo: Cyril (born Constantine, c. 827-869) and Methodius (c. 815-885) were brothers native to Thessalonica (Greek Salonica), a Byzantine city in whose region a Slavic language was spoken. Around 862, Prince Rastislav of Great Moravia asked Emperor Michael III and Patriarch Photius for missionaries capable of proclaiming the Gospel in the Slavic language, and not in Latin or Greek. The choice fell on the two brothers, who knew the local language. To translate the liturgical and biblical texts, they created an alphabet of their own, the Glagolitic, the first writing system designed for the phonetic particularities of Slavic. Cyril was also a scholar: years earlier (851) he had been sent on a diplomatic mission to Caliph Al-Mutawakkil, and in 860 he had taken part in a mission to the Khazars.

itens.resumo: Anglo-Saxon monk who, from 719, evangelized the Germanic peoples, felled Thor's sacred oak at Geismar, and was martyred in Frisia in 754.
itens.corpo:
Boniface, born Winfrid (c. 672/675, in the region of Exeter, in the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Wessex), was a Benedictine monk and scholar when he felt the missionary call to the Continent. In 718-719 he went to Rome, where Pope Gregory II commissioned him to evangelize the Germanic peoples and gave him the name Boniface, that is, 'one who does good'. He settled mainly in Hesse and Thuringia, where he reorganized Christian communities that had lost contact with the hierarchy of the Church.

The most famous episode of his mission took place around 723, in Gaesmere (present-day Geismar, in Hesse), according to the eighth-century account in Willibald's Vita Bonifatii. Before a crowd of pagans, Boniface felled the great oak consecrated to the god Thor (called Donar or, in the Roman interpretatio, 'Jupiter's oak'). The tree fell, and tradition says it split into four pieces. With the wood, he had a chapel dedicated to Saint Peter built on the site, the nucleus of the future cathedral of Fritzlar. The event is regarded as the starting point of the formal Christianization of Germania.

Boniface reorganized the Frankish and Germanic Church: he was made a bishop (722), received the pallium from Gregory III (732), became papal legate for Germania (737-738), and was the first Archbishop of Mainz, in 745. He founded or consolidated dioceses such as Büraburg, Würzburg, and Erfurt, as well as Salzburg, Regensburg, Freising, and Passau in Bavaria. His disciple Sturm founded the Abbey of Fulda in 742, where Boniface would be buried.

In 754, already elderly, he returned to Frisia to resume the conversion of the Frisians. He arranged a meeting for the confirmation of new baptized converts near Dokkum, but instead of the converts, a band of armed pagans appeared and killed him, together with about fifty companions, on June 5. His body was taken to Fulda. Saint Boniface is venerated as a martyr by the Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church, with his feast on June 5.
