itens.resumo: Korean Catholics martyred in the persecutions of 1839, 1846 and 1866, canonized by John Paul II in Seoul on May 6, 1984, during the bicentennial of the Korean Church.
itens.corpo:
The Catholic Church in Korea was born without foreign missionaries: in 1784, Yi Seung-Hun, who had returned from China, became the first known Korean to embrace the faith, bringing crucifixes, rosaries and images. Over the following two decades, Catholicism grew clandestinely, led largely by lay people, who saw in it a doctrine in which all people stood on the same level, in contrast with the rigid Confucian hierarchy of Joseon society.

This expansion drew persecution. Korean believers suffered three great waves of repression, in 1839, 1846 and 1866. The best-known name is that of Andrew Kim Taegon (1821-1846), the first Korean Catholic priest. Chosen as a seminarian at the age of fifteen, he was sent to Macau to study and, after being ordained a priest in Shanghai in 1845, returned to Joseon aboard a small wooden boat, working to secure safe routes of entry for missionaries during the persecution. Arrested shortly afterward, he was martyred by beheading on September 16, 1846, on the banks of the Han River, at Saenamteo, at the age of 25.

Alongside him, Paul Chong Hasang and other martyrs are venerated, of whom 103 were canonized together. John Paul II himself presided at the canonization in Seoul on May 6, 1984, during his apostolic journey to Korea, when the 200th anniversary of the first Korean convert was being commemorated. It was the first canonization celebrated outside Rome.

The site of the execution, in Seoul, became the Jeoldu-san Shrine ('beheading mountain'), erected in 1967 as a memorial and pilgrimage center. The memorial of the Korean martyrs is celebrated on September 20, and the spread of their veneration is also linked to the World Youth Day in Seoul, scheduled for 2027.

itens.titulo: Saint Nino and the Christianization of Iberia (Georgia)
itens.resumo: A Cappadocian woman who, in the 4th century, preached Christianity in Iberia (present-day Georgia), converted King Mirian III, and created the grapevine cross, the symbol of the Georgian Church.
itens.corpo:
The conversion of the Caucasian kingdom of Iberia — the ancient name of present-day Georgia, also called Kartli — is linked to a woman: Saint Nino (c. 296-c. 338/340). According to the hagiographical tradition, she was born in Cappadocia, the daughter of Zabulon — said to be a brother of the great martyr Saint George — and of Susanna, sister of the Patriarch of Jerusalem. She is said to have gone to Iberia moved by the desire to venerate the tunic of Christ, but the purpose she attributed to the Virgin Mary was the evangelization of that people.

Nino is depicted with an unmistakable attribute: the grapevine cross. The account tells that she dreamed of the Virgin, who gave her a cross made of two vine branches; Nino bound them together with her own hair. This cross, with its arms slightly slanting downward, is to this day the symbol of the Georgian Orthodox Church, and the episode expresses the inculturation of the faith in a land of wine.

According to the Georgian chronicles and the account 'Conversion of Georgia', Nino baptized King Mirian III (Meribanes) and his wife, Queen Nana, which set off the baptism of Kartli and its inhabitants. Byzantine historians such as Rufinus of Aquileia, Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen, and Theodoret of Cyrus mention the episode, although they describe Nino as an unidentified Roman captive, and not as the daughter of Zabulon. The date of the baptism is disputed: some sources point to around 337, others to the 320s.

The Georgian Church, relying on Byzantine sources, maintains that the spread of Christianity in the region began earlier, with the Apostle Andrew, the First-Called, considered its founder. Archaeological excavations reinforce the antiquity of the local faith: in 3rd-century graves, seals appear bearing crosses, fish, and anchors, early Christian symbols. Saint Nino is venerated as isapostolos (equal to the apostles) and patroness of Georgia.

itens.titulo: Alexandre de Rhodes, Jesuit Missionary in Vietnam
itens.resumo: French Jesuit (Avignon, 1591 – Isfahan, 1660) who evangelized Tonkin and Cochinchina and systematized the Latin alphabet for Vietnamese, the quốc ngữ, with his dictionary and catechism published in Rome in 1651.
itens.corpo:
Alexandre de Rhodes was born in Avignon, then part of the Papal States, on March 15, 1591. He entered the Society of Jesus in Rome on April 24, 1612 and, after his ordination, set out for the missions of the East. He arrived in Cochinchina in 1624, studying the local language under the guidance of the Portuguese Jesuit Francisco de Pina; he learned it so quickly that within a few months he was already able to preach in Vietnamese. In 1627, at the request of his superiors, he began the mission in Tonkin (Đàng Ngoài), in the north of present-day Vietnam, where he worked until 1630.

During those three years, Rhodes resided at the court of Hanoi, under the lords Trịnh Tùng and Trịnh Tráng, whom he impressed with gifts such as a clock of complex engineering and a gilded volume of mathematics. He himself estimated that he had baptized between six and seven thousand Vietnamese in this period. In 1630, however, he was expelled from the kingdom: mandarins jealous of their power convinced the local lord that Christian doctrine threatened an authority grounded in Confucianism, and an edict unfavorable to Christians was issued. He then withdrew to Macau, where he spent about ten years teaching philosophy, before returning to southern Vietnam between 1640 and 1646, when he was condemned to death, a sentence later commuted to perpetual exile.

In forced exile, he devoted himself to the lexicographical work that would become his lasting mark. He compiled the Dictionarium Annamiticum Lusitanum et Latinum, the first trilingual Vietnamese–Portuguese–Latin dictionary, and the catechism Phép giảng tám ngày ("Instruction in eight days"), both printed in Rome in 1651 by the press of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Propaganda Fide). These works, together with his grammar of the Annamite language, fixed and refined the romanized writing system for Vietnamese, the quốc ngữ, begun by earlier Portuguese missionaries. It should be noted that Rhodes was not its sole inventor: he was the decisive link in a chain of scholars, and the quốc ngữ would only become the official and widespread script of the country in the twentieth century, long after his death.

In 1652–1654, Rhodes was in Europe, chiefly in France (Marseille, Lyon and Paris), with three declared aims: to convince the Pope of the urgency of sending bishops to Tonkin and Cochinchina, to seek material assistance from Christian princes, and to ask for more missionaries for Asia. His efforts had weight in the creation of the Paris Foreign Missions Society (MEP), which would later take over the evangelization of Vietnam. He also left the account Divers voyages et missions du P. Alexandre de Rhodes (Paris, 1653), an important source on seventeenth-century Vietnam. He died in Isfahan, Persia, on November 5, 1660, on his way to the East.

itens.titulo: Bartolomé de las Casas and the Peaceful Evangelization of the Americas
itens.resumo: Spanish Dominican friar (1484–1566), Bishop of Chiapas and 'Protector of the Indians', who argued that the indigenous peoples should be evangelized by persuasion and not by force, a thesis he upheld in the Valladolid debate against Sepúlveda.
itens.corpo:
Bartolomé de las Casas (Seville, November 11, 1484 – Madrid, July 18, 1566) arrived in the New World as a layman and became a Dominican friar. He was appointed the first resident Bishop of Chiapas, in present-day Mexico, and the first officially designated 'Protector of the Indians' by the Spanish Crown. His conversion from exploiting colonist to critic of the conquest is narrated by himself in his works, above all in A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (written in 1542, published in Seville in 1552) and in the History of the Indies, in which he denounced the abuses committed by the conquistadors against the native peoples.

At the center of his thought was a missionary thesis: the Christian faith can only be proclaimed by peaceful preaching, by example, and by persuasion, never by war or coercion. His treatise De unico vocationis modo ("The Only Way of Drawing All Peoples to the True Religion") maintains that forced conversion is invalid and contrary to the Gospel. This doctrine was linked to the bull Sublimis Deus, promulgated by Pope Paul III on June 2, 1537, which declared the indigenous peoples of the Americas to be rational beings, capable of receiving the faith, forbade their enslavement, and affirmed that the preaching of the Gospel was to be carried out peacefully.

The high point and most famous moment of this controversy was the Valladolid Debate (1550–1551), held at the Colegio de San Gregorio in Spain and convened by Charles V. Before theologians and jurists, Las Casas confronted the humanist and royal chronicler Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, who defended the right to subjugate the indigenous peoples by force, claiming that they were 'slaves by nature' and that war would bring them benefits. Las Casas replied by citing Scripture and canon law, and his argument, summed up in the phrase 'all the peoples of the world are men', convinced the theologians that Spanish policy was unjust. The debate, however, reached no conclusive formal decision, and in practice it did little to restrain the colonists, who continued to exploit the indigenous peoples.

The memory of Las Casas remains alive and controversial. His defense of the dignity of the native peoples made him a reference point for later theology and missionary thought (the Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez, father of liberation theology, devoted a celebrated study to him), while his Short Account was, in later centuries, exploited by Spain's rival powers in the so-called 'Black Legend'. Be that as it may, his insistence that evangelization must be inseparable from respect for the freedom and life of the peoples evangelized remains a fundamental landmark in the history of missions.
